title: Intraspecific variability in feather moult extent declines under both low and high constraints
content:

Abstract

Intraspecific trait variability (ITV) is a fundamental feature of biological populations and the raw material upon which natural selection acts, yet its drivers remain poorly understood. We examined how environmental and intrinsic constraints shape ITV in a key avian morphological trait—the extent of feather moult—which directly affects an individual's future appearance, and thus its attractiveness, competitive ability, and overall fitness. Using data from 21,050 individuals across 219 passerine species, collected through fieldwork and from zoological collections, we quantified variation in the extent of feather replacement during post-juvenile and pre-breeding moults and developed a time extremity index (TEx) representing the degree of constraint on the time available for feather renewal. Phylogenetic models revealed that ITV in moult extent declined when TEx values were high, corresponding to either highly constrained or highly permissive conditions, and peaked at low TEx values, representing intermediate conditions, with stronger effects observed in post-juvenile than in pre-breeding moult. These results demonstrate that extreme environmental or life history constraints limit individual responses and reduce phenotypic variability, while intermediate conditions foster greater diversity in moult patterns and trait expression. This pattern suggests that moderate environmental pressures allow for the coexistence of multiple adaptive solutions within populations, enhancing ecological flexibility. Our findings provide empirical evidence for an extremity-dependent association between environmental constraints and intraspecific variation, emphasizing that variability itself is context-dependent. This pattern may help explain why populations facing moderate, rather than extreme, ecological pressures often display the highest potential for morphological flexibility and adaptive diversity.
